ask/ask: A classifier looks at an image and answers class zero. But which parts of the image made it say so?
ask/pixels: This image has just four pixels, the dots an image is made of. Their brightnesses make the input, x: three, one, two and one.
ask/nudge: To find out, brighten a single pixel by one unit, and watch class zero's score, s zero. Pixel zero: s zero rises by one.
ask/jump: Pixel one: it falls by three, all the way down to minus one.
ask/still: Pixel two: it does not move at all. Pixel three: it rises by two.
ask/grad: How fast s zero moves per unit of brightness, pixel by pixel, is its gradient with respect to x, partial s zero, partial x.
ask/name: Paint how far each nudge moved the score onto its pixel: that is a saliency map. Salient means standing out: these pixels stand out to the classifier.
linear/open: Why those numbers? The classifier is linear: W has one row of weights per class, and the scores, s, are W times x.
linear/row: Class zero's score is row zero dotted with x. Raise pixel one by a unit, and only its own term moves, by its weight: the minus three the nudge found.
linear/grad: So the gradient of s zero is just row zero. The pixel values drop out, so the map is the same for any image.
linear/bias: A bias drops out too: no pixel appears in it.
linear/history: That is where Karen Simonyan, Andrea Vedaldi and Andrew Zisserman, at Oxford, began in 2013: for a linear score, the size of each weight says how much its pixel matters.
map/sign: The sign of each partial says which way the score moves; its size, how fast. Minus three is as fast as plus three, just downward.
map/abs: So the map keeps each size and drops the sign: the absolute value, written between two bars. One, three, zero, two.
map/show: Pixel one glows brightest: it is the map's argmax, the position of its largest entry. Pixel two, with weight zero, stays dark.
map/adds: Pixel zero is the brightest, and adds the most to the score right now. But the map asks how fast the score moves, not what a pixel adds.
map/other: Each class has its own map, from its own row. Class two's row, minus one, zero, three, minus two, lights up pixel two instead.
deeper/deep: A deeper model's score is no weighted sum, so there is no row to read. But a nudge still moves it at some rate, and Simonyan's team used just that: near one image, the gradient plays the part of the weights.
deeper/graph: Here is a small one. Pixel zero is doubled, pixel one is multiplied by minus one, and an add makes q.
deeper/max: A max gate keeps q or zero, whichever is larger, and a multiply by three makes the score, s.
deeper/fwd: Forward, on the image two, one: q is three, the max keeps it, and s is nine.
deeper/back: Now walk back from s, starting at one. The multiply by three hands back three.
deeper/route: The max routes all of it on, since q beat zero, and the add copies it to both inputs.
deeper/px0: Pixel zero was doubled, so it gets two times three: six.
deeper/px1: Pixel one was multiplied by minus one, so it gets minus three. Saliency: six and three.
deeper/once: One walk back found both. A whole map takes a single backward pass, which is why Simonyan's team called it extremely quick.
deeper/depends: Unlike the linear case, this map depends on the image. On the image one, three, q is minus one, the max routes nothing back, and both saliencies are zero.
deeper/paths: And if a pixel reaches the score along two paths, its gradients from the two of them add.
